newsitem.title: UK: UK survey shows SBC Warburg as City favourite.
newsitem.headline: UK survey shows SBC Warburg as City favourite.

text.p: SBC Warburg toppled NatWest Securities to regain its place as the favourite stockbroker amongst fund managers, according to an influential survey published on Wednesday.
A top position in the annual Extel survey is important both for winning business from investing institutions and for brokers' own careers.

SBC Warburg, whose five-year winning streak ended last year with a drop to third place, led this year by a comfortable margin. NatWest Securities, the broking arm of Britain's troubled NatWest Markets, slipped to second position while Merrill Lynch leapt to third place from sixth last year.

The Extel survey, which has been produced for 24 years, was compiled by questioning 105 fund mangers in charge of well over 1,000 billion pounds ($1.7 trillion) of shares about which analysts they rate most highly. The overall response rate was 61 percent, but Extel said 71 percent of those managing funds of over 20 billion pounds responded.
The survey shows the rankings of the top research brokers and their analysts weighted by size of funds under management by the respondents who voted for them.
The league tables are based on the weighted results. Only 2.3 percent of the votes separated the top five brokers and 80 percent of votes went to the top eight brokers in the all sectors, Extel said.

After last year's gain in votes, HSBC James Capel lost ground and dropped from second place in 1996 to fifth in the 1997 all sectors league. UBS Limited retained its fourth position, with BZW dropping to sixth from fifth place last year.

Dresdner Kleinwort Benson stayed at seventh and ABN AMRO Hoare Govett kept eighth place in the league. Goldman Sachs International regained votes and moved back to ninth, with Morgan Stanley International slipping to tenth position.
In the UK sectors league, SBC Warburg again stole first place from NatWest Securities, who moved to second position.

The league table for research of pan-European industry sectors, including Britain, ranked NatWest first with a relatively strong lead, ahead of SBC Warburg and Merrill Lynch. This was weighted by funds under management and market capitalisation.

In the European continent sectors league, SBC Warburg again ranked top, and with a much bigger margin. NatWest Securities moved back into second place ousting UBS Limited, ranked second in 1995, into fourth place. Goldman Sachs International jumped to third from seventh place in 1996.

For the fourth year running, the 1997 "All Stars" rating for the top ranked team in Britain went to Fergus MacLeod's "Oil, Integrated" team at NatWest Securities. HSBC James Capel's pharmaceutical analysts, led by Andrew Tivenan, won the top ranked European sector team weighted by market capitalisation.
The top votes for an individual analyst again went to Fergus MacLeod while runner up was Charles Burrows who covers the engineering sectors for HSBC James Capel.
The survey showed that 51 percent of the respondents found pan-European research of "some importance" to them, up from 39 percent last year.
A total 45 percent of respondents said they had increased the amount of research they were doing in-house and 51 percent said they planned to increase it over the next year.
Geoffrey Osmint, founder and consulting editor of the

Extel Survey, told a lunchtime presentation of the awards there was evidence that some fund managers were concerned over analysts spending too much time on corporate finance. He cited Dresdner Morgan Grenfell and HSBC James Capel as particular examples.
Osmint also noted a shift towards pan-European and global research.
John Parrott of Commercial Union told representatives at the awards ceremony that this trend could lead to UK-orientated funds such as his slipping down the league tables of performance in time.
($ = 0.602 British Pounds)
